name: Chipsi mayai
description: Chips (French fries) fried in a pan with beaten eggs until they set into a thick omelette, sometimes with onion and bell pepper. It was invented on the streets of Dar es Salaam in the 1980s and is often called Tanzania's unofficial national dish. Also known as zege.
how_to_eat: Eat it hot with kachumbari salad and pili pili hot sauce, or with tomato sauce and mayonnaise.
how_to_order: Made to order at street stalls; several sellers work at Forodhani Gardens in Stone Town.

name: Ugali with dagaa
description: Ugali served with dagaa, small sardine-like fish that are sun-dried and cooked with onion, tomato, lime and chilli. Freshwater dagaa come from Lakes Victoria, Tanganyika and Nyasa; in Dar es Salaam the Indian Ocean dagaa mchele are usually fried rather than stewed.
how_to_eat: Pinch off ugali and use it to scoop up the dagaa.
how_to_order: Ask for ugali dagaa at local eateries; in Dar es Salaam ask whether the dagaa is fried or stewed.

name: Wali na maharage
description: Rice and beans, an everyday Tanzanian meal. The beans (kidney or soy) are often stewed with onion, tomato, spices and coconut milk and served with greens such as mchicha. It is also made for holidays, weddings, religious festivals and funerals.
how_to_eat: Eat with a spoon, often with greens such as mchicha on the side.
how_to_order: Found at local eateries; ask for maharage ya nazi for the coconut-bean version.

name: Kisamvu
description: Cassava leaves pounded with garlic, onion, ginger and chilli, simmered for hours, then finished with coconut milk into a thick stew. A daily staple in Zanzibari households, usually served with ugali or rice.
how_to_eat: Eat with ugali (ugali kisamvu) or rice.
how_to_order: Usually served as a side at local eateries; ask whether any meat or stock is added if vegetarian.

name: Vitumbua
description: Small, slightly sweet pancakes of lightly fermented rice-flour batter with coconut milk and cardamom, cooked in a special pan with round moulds. A common Tanzanian snack.
how_to_order: Sold by street vendors, several pieces at a time.

name: Kashata
description: Crunchy bars of grated coconut or peanuts cooked in sugar, sometimes with cardamom, cinnamon or nutmeg. On the coast a piece is traditionally eaten between sips of unsweetened black coffee.
how_to_eat: Take a small bite between sips of strong black coffee.
how_to_order: Sold by street vendors and coffee sellers; ask if it is the coconut or peanut kind.

name: Mchemsho
description: A clear broth of meat (beef, tripe, chicken or goat) boiled with potatoes, green bananas, carrots, onion, peppers and chilli, finished with lime. Mchemsho is a family of boiled dishes; it is eaten at any time of day and is a popular hangover cure.
how_to_eat: Drink the broth and eat the meat and vegetables.
how_to_order: Ask for mchemsho at local eateries and say which meat you want.

name: Konyagi
description: A clear Tanzanian spirit (35% ABV) with citrus notes from a proprietary flavour blend, first distilled in 1970 and made by Tanzania Distilleries, part of Tanzania Breweries. It is marketed as "The Spirit of the Nation".
how_to_order: Sold in bars and shops in 750, 500 and 200 ml bottles.

name: Zanzibar pizza
description: A thin dough folded into a square parcel around minced beef or chicken, onion, peppers, egg, soft cheese and mayonnaise, then fried on a griddle; it is closer to a murtabak than an Italian pizza. It is a staple of the stalls at Stone Town's Forodhani Gardens night market.
how_to_eat: Eat it hot off the griddle with chilli sauce.
how_to_order: Choose your filling at the stalls in Forodhani Gardens, which set up around sunset.

name: Urojo (Zanzibar mix)
description: A tangy, turmeric-yellow soup thickened with flour and soured with mango or tamarind, ladled over toppings such as bhajia fritters, potato balls, cassava crisps, chickpeas, boiled egg and small beef skewers, then finished with coconut chutney and chilli. Sold at Zanzibar street stands and Forodhani night market, and also in Dar es Salaam.
how_to_eat: Eat with a spoon, mixing the toppings into the soup as you go.
how_to_order: Ask for urojo or "Zanzibar mix" at Forodhani Gardens or street stands in Stone Town; say if you want it without meat.

name: Mkate wa kumimina
description: A Zanzibari rice bread: soaked, ground rice (or rice flour) mixed with coconut milk, sugar, cardamom, egg and yeast, left to rise and baked into a soft, slightly sweet round cake. A similar Swahili rice bread is called mkate wa sinia.
how_to_eat: Eat a slice as an afternoon snack with black tea or chai.

name: Pweza wa nazi
description: Octopus slowly cooked until tender, then simmered in coconut milk with garlic, lime and spices such as curry, cardamom and cinnamon. Octopus is caught by spear-fishers, and is also sold grilled on skewers (mishkaki) in Stone Town.
how_to_order: Order at Zanzibar restaurants; Intrepid warns that pre-cooked octopus skewers at night stalls can be risky when reheated.

name: Zanzibar chocolate
description: A chewy bar of toasted sesame seeds bound with honey and cut into small diamonds; despite the name it contains no cocoa.
how_to_order: Sold in small bags by street vendors around Stone Town.

name: Zanzibar spiced coffee
description: Strong black Arabic-style coffee, unsweetened and flavoured with ginger or cardamom, sold by vendors with brass pots in small cups. Stone Town's Jaws Corner is the classic place where men gather over it in the morning to talk.
how_to_eat: Sip it quickly and alternate with bites of sweet peanut brittle.
how_to_order: Buy a cup from street coffee sellers, especially at Jaws Corner in Stone Town.

name: Sugarcane juice
description: Fresh juice pressed from sugarcane to order, sometimes with ginger or lime. It is sold cheaply from carts and roadside stalls in Stone Town.
how_to_order: Ask the vendor to add ginger or lime when they press it.

name: Ndizi nyama
description: A stew of green cooking bananas and beef with potatoes, simmered in coconut milk. The name means "bananas with meat"; it is a classic of the Chagga people on the slopes of Kilimanjaro, who are known for growing bananas.
how_to_eat: Eat with a spoon, often with sliced avocado on the side.
how_to_order: Ask for ndizi nyama at local eateries; meatless versions exist.

name: Mtori
description: A thick soup of green bananas and beef, often with potatoes and sometimes milk or cream, boiled and then mashed smooth. It comes from the Chagga of the Kilimanjaro (Moshi-Arusha) area and is eaten in the morning for energy; Maasai women also eat it during postpartum confinement.
how_to_eat: Eat it as a main meal at breakfast, lunch or dinner.

name: Machalari
description: A Chagga stew of green bananas; one source describes it with beef, while a Machame cultural-tourism cooking class lists it as a banana and vegetable dish.
how_to_order: Taught in Chagga cooking classes on the slopes of Kilimanjaro; ask whether it contains meat.

name: Kiburu
description: A Chagga dish of bananas cooked with beans, one of the banana-based home dishes of the Kilimanjaro region.

name: Mbege
description: A mildly alcoholic (about 1-3%) beer of the Chagga people, made by cooking mashed bananas for hours, fermenting them for up to a week and mixing in finger-millet porridge. It is sweet with a slightly sour aftertaste.
how_to_order: Hard to find outside northern Tanzania; Machame village tours include brewing demonstrations and tastings.

name: Makande
description: A one-pot stew of maize kernels and beans slow-cooked for hours, traditionally in a clay pot, with onion, peppers and carrots; the makande ya nazi version is simmered in coconut milk. Matador links it to the Iraqw people of the Ngorongoro Highlands.
how_to_eat: Eat with a spoon as a filling main.
how_to_order: Ask for makande (or makande ya nazi) at local eateries.

name: Kilimanjaro coffee
description: Arabica coffee grown on the slopes of Kilimanjaro and Mount Meru, a key cash crop of the Chagga people.
how_to_order: Many farms on Kilimanjaro's slopes offer guided tours during the harvest season.

name: Senene (fried grasshoppers)
description: Longhorn grasshoppers (bush crickets) trapped with lights in swarms after the April and November rains, then fried. They are a prized Haya delicacy in Kagera, offered to guests as a sign of respect, and a lucrative seasonal cash crop around Bukoba.
how_to_order: Sold fresh or deep-fried by street vendors and shops around Bukoba in season; fried senene keeps for months and is also sold in Dar es Salaam.

name: Matoke (ndizi Bukoba)
description: Green bananas steamed in banana leaves, then mashed or cooked with beef, tripe or smoked fish, beans or groundnuts. It is the staple of the Haya people of Kagera.
how_to_order: Ask for ndizi or matoke at local eateries in Bukoba; ask what it is cooked with.

name: Nile perch (sangara)
description: Nile perch, the large Lake Victoria fish called sangara in Tanzania, served grilled, fried or stewed (mchuzi wa samaki) with ugali or rice. With tilapia it is the everyday fish of the Lake Zone.
how_to_order: Order it grilled or fried at lakeshore eateries in Mwanza.

name: Samaki na viazi vitamu
description: Tilapia cut into pieces and boiled with sweet potatoes, onion, tomato, carrot and a little chilli into a mild broth. A Lake Zone dish, adapted on the coast with snapper, coconut milk and turmeric.
